claims.text: High configurational entropy intrinsically slows bulk atomic diffusion in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Nanoscale confinement contributes to sluggish atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Sluggish diffusion minimizes phase separation and thereby preserves structural and chemical stability at high service temperatures.
A high-binding-energy ligand-exchange treatment can produce a passivating surface layer on the nanoparticles.
The passivation layer modifies the nanoparticle surface-energy state.
The modified surface-energy state suppresses surface diffusion.
Suppressing surface diffusion reduces particle coarsening.
The passivation layer suppresses chemical segregation.
The engineered surface layer suppresses oxidation during high-temperature exposure.
The combined effects of slow bulk diffusion and suppressed surface processes stabilize the single-phase nanoparticle structure during prolonged high-temperature service.
Passivated nanoparticles will coarsen less than untreated nanoparticles under identical thermal exposure.
Passivated nanoparticles will show less compositional segregation than untreated nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will retain their single-phase structure better than untreated nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will retain functional properties better than untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies across 773–1173 K for catalytic use and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use.
The surrounding atmosphere, particularly inert versus oxidizing conditions, influences nanoparticle stability.
Aggressive oxidation or unusually large surface-energy fluctuations can overwhelm the proposed stabilization mechanism.
Chemical ordering or segregation can affect thermal conductivity in a near-equiatomic multielement alloy.
High-temperature processing can change the phase constitution and ordering of multielement high-entropy alloys.
